utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] [no translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you all, and before we proceed, I would like to introduce to you the other two Judges that compose this Trial Chamber. To my right is Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and to my left, Judge Taya from Japan. Thank you. There are a few preliminaries that I would like to touch upon before we start our labours and before I give the floor to the Prosecutor, Joanna Korner, and what I will be saying is partly to address you to some of the practices and policies that will be adopted by this Trial Chamber in the course of this trial. The whole idea is that it is the opinion of this Trial Chamber that you should not exactly be forewarned but you should be advised beforehand of what to expect given certain circumstances, particularly with regard to evidence and with regard to procedure, so that there will be no room for discussion, further discussion, at a later time. But before I move to these points, I would like to address the accused in this trial, Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic, and draw their attention to Article 21 of the Statute of this Tribunal, which spells out a number of procedural guarantees in a human rights fair trial and due process context that I suppose they have been made aware of already. But since this is the beginning of the trial - in other words, this is another phase of the proceedings and perhaps the most crucial phase of the proceedings taken by this Tribunal against the two accused - I am going to refer to the basic points of Article 21. Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic, in terms of part 1, clause 1, of Article 21 of the Statute, all persons shall be equal before this Tribunal, and in the determination of the charges that have been brought against you under the indictment as now finally amended, you are entitled, in terms of part 2 of Article 21, to a fair and public hearing, subject, of course, to what is stated in Article 22 of the Statute, which I don't think is the case for me to go into. You will be reminded later on as well, when I come to something else, that under clause 3 of Article 21, you are presumed innocent until you are proven guilty according to the provisions of the same Statute that regulates the works and the constitution and the workings of this Tribunal. Then, in the determination of any charge against you pursuant to the Statute, you are entitled to the following minimum guarantees -- and I emphasise the word "minimum" guarantees, because there will be other guarantees that you will be -- you will benefit from as we go along, and these are guarantees that more or less universally now and particularly in Europe are considered to be essential for a fair trial. But basically, the first requirement - and I suppose this has already been more or less satisfied, even though challenged in the past - is to be informed promptly and in detail in a language which you understand of the nature and cause of the charges brought against you. Then - and, again, this is something that we have discussed and debated and which we will probably need to debate later on as well - you are entitled to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of your Defence and to communicate with a counsel of your own choosing. You are also entitled to be tried without undue delay, and you can rest assured that this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber will do its utmost to finish this case as speedily as possibly but with all due respect to your other rights. You also have a right to be tried not in absentia but in your presence and to defend yourselves in person or through legal assistance of your own choosing. You are also entitled to be informed, if at any time you do not have any legal assistance, of this right. I hope we will not have to come to that, but if it ever happens in the course of this trial, you will obviously be reminded of your rights. You also have a right to have legal assistance assigned to you in any case where the interests of justice require and without payment, in any such case, if you do not have sufficient means to pay for your defence. Then something which is very important and which your lawyers definitely know more than you do: You have a right to examine and to have examined the witnesses brought here against you and to -- also you have a right to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on your own behalf, under the same conditions as those witnesses which are brought to testify against you. This also means, although it is not stated, that you also have a right to bring forward any documents, any exhibits that you consider necessary in your defence, subject, of course, to various rules of evidence that govern trials like this one. You have also the right for the free assistance of an interpreter if you do not understand or speak the language which at any time is used during the proceedings. I see that we have a team of interpreters, translators, here. If at any time in the course of the trial you encounter difficulties in this, please do not hesitate. Interrupt me and my colleagues and whoever would be in possession of the floor at the time and let us know, because it is very important that at any given moment, you are fully aware of what is taking place. Then finally, you may -- you have a right not to be compelled to testify against yourselves or to confess any guilt, which brings me to something -- to the first point that I wanted to touch upon, that is, this right to silence and also privilege against self-incrimination. I have just told you that in terms of Article 21, you have -- there is a very important principle that will certainly govern all these proceedings, namely, that you are both presumed innocent until found guilty and that the burden of proving your guilt rests generally with the Prosecution. As a necessary consequence of this, we have a corollary principle, namely, that you have a fundamental right to remain silent throughout the whole trial if you choose to. You also enjoy a privilege against self-incrimination, which this trial will guarantee to you. The whole purpose of this right to remain silent and the raison d'etre of the privilege against self-incrimination are meant to protect you from being compelled to testify against your own will, against your own interest, or to confess any guilt. I also wish to affirm that it is not permissible for the Prosecution in the course of this trial to make any adverse inferences based on your silence. However, you should keep in mind that should, at a later stage, you decide voluntarily to offer your own testimony, your own evidence, then more or less, with some exceptions that have been highlighted in previous case law of this Tribunal, you will be in the same position as any other witness and be treated accordingly. In other words, if you take the witness box and you make the solemn declaration to say -- to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, this is precisely what will be expected from you. There is, of course, a question that was raised by the learned Prosecutor during the last phase or last part of Monday's session of the Pre-Trial Conference as to what is expected from you should you at a later stage decide it is in your interest to offer your own testimony. When should you do this? I know that the practice in this Tribunal has not been always the same, in other words, there has been a variation on the same thing. But it is desirable that if you decide to give evidence, you will give evidence before any of the other witnesses that you intend to produce in your own defence. I'm telling you this in your own interest. And in this context, I would also like to remind you that in the only two other instances that I can remember when the accused, the respondent, or the defendant decided to give evidence after all the other witnesses for the Defence had given evidence, it was made very clear to the accused that the probative value of his or her evidence in those circumstances might suffer. I repeat the same advice, not a warning: This Chamber as composed would expect you, if you decide to give evidence, to give evidence before all the other witnesses for the Defence. If you opt not to, if you opt to give evidence later, you may be faced with this problem. Leading questions. I think we should -- we opted to be open on this straight away, play our cards openly. This is an area where the practice of this Tribunal also has not always been constant. But I will tell you how this Trial Chamber in the course of this trial will deal with leading questions. This Trial Chamber in the course of this trial will not allow leading questions during examination-in-chief or a direct examination of a witness. To make myself clear, also because I realise that we have counsel coming from different legal traditions - and I come from a legal culture which has succeeded in mixing the two - I will explain to you what I mean by a leading question, what I understand by a leading question, at least for the purpose of these proceedings. And a leading question to me - and to us, actually - is a question framed in such a manner as to suggest to the witness the answer required from him or from her. There will be some exceptions which will be applied to this strict rule, and these exceptions are based on the prior jurisprudence of this Tribunal and also on the practice that more or less has been adopted in the past with regard to leading questions. First, there will be exception to this rule where a witness affirms a certain fact and another witness is called for the purpose of confronting or contradicting that witness. The latter may be asked, in direct terms, whether that particular fact ever took place. Also, questions which are merely introductory to others, that are material or which relate to undisputed matters, will be in general terms allowed to be asked in direct terms without objection. Also, leading questions will be allowed to be put where the party calling the witness is given leave to treat that witness as an adverse or a hostile witness. Leading questions will, of course, be allowed for matters which are not contested. Leading questions will also, on a case-by-case basis, be allowed in cases of witnesses who happen to have a limited understanding. We hope to have very few of these. And leading questions will also be allowed in cases of a witness whose recollection has been exhausted but who there is reason to believe should be in possession or know additional facts material to the case. Finally - this is where the practice of this Tribunal has not been always constant - finally, leading questions will always be applied upon cross-examination. So I'm making this very clear: It applies equally to Defence and to Prosecution. While it has been the practice in some Trial Chambers not to allow direct questions, leading questions, upon cross-examination, this will not be the system adopted by this Trial Chamber. So I'm making that clear to you at the very outset. Hearsay evidence. Now, as you know, this is a rule with which practitioners in common law jurisdictions are very familiar. It is obviously something that has come up on several occasions before this Tribunal in different cases, and it is something on which this Tribunal has pronounced itself. More or less I'm informing you that this Trial Chamber in the course of this trial will adopt the jurisprudence of this Tribunal on the matter. What -- I will be more precise. Basically, the governing rule is that contained in paragraph (C) of Rule 89, which makes it clear that this Trial Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have relevance. Also, this International Tribunal, as pointed out in the Blaskic case, is a sui generis one with its own rules and procedure and which does not merely constitute a transposition of national legal systems. In fact, these last years have shown this Tribunal to be heading towards more or less a hybrid system, and this has a bearing on the way this Chamber will deal with the aspect of hearsay evidence. The rule of -- against hearsay evidence in criminal cases, as this Trial Chamber understands it, is in the following terms: Namely, former statements of any person, whether or not he or she is a witness in the proceedings, may not be given in evidence if the purpose is to tender them as evidence of the truth of the matters asserted in them, unless they were made by a defendant and constitute admissions of fact relevant to those proceedings. However, in the Aleksovski case, this Tribunal defined hearsay evidence in a more restricted manner; namely, the statement of a person made otherwise than in proceedings in which it has been tendered but nevertheless being tendered in those proceedings in order to establish the truth of what that person states -- says. The position that this Trial Chamber will be adopting in this trial is that hearsay evidence - which in any case has never been considered to be an absolute rule even in common law jurisdictions - will not be considered inadmissible or made subject to any prohibition in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. principle, subject, of course, to it being deemed relevant and having a probative value in the first place. Two minor points that are more or less related, though they are complementary, though one does not exhaust the other: I would imagine that both the Prosecution and the Defence will encounter the phenomenon of hostile witnesses. Sometimes it happens, and when it happens, it creates problems, problems in the sense that you would be prepared one way in examining or cross-examining that -- in examining that witness, which you yourself would have produced, and which might take you by surprise. The rule that will be applied by this Trial Chamber is that a party producing a witness - we are talking of the witness that you yourself have produced - will not be allowed to attack the credibility of that witness without the permission of the Trial Chamber. In other words, first, you have to ask for the permission of this Trial Chamber to treat that witness as an adverse witness, as a hostile witness. Given that permission, then you would be able to treat that witness as a hostile one, or as an adverse one - the Americans prefer to use the word "adverse" rather than "hostile," I understand - and in this context, contradict that witness by other evidence, even evidence that may have been tendered in previous occasions. That brings me to the second point, the use, permitted use, that will be made of prior statements. The rule that will be followed by this Trial Chamber is that prior, out-of-court statements will be allowed along the lines indicated and decided in Prosecutor versus Pocka ^ Papic? Prcac?. In other words, the rule will be that the principle of the orality of debates, in other words, that evidence more or less as a rule should be tendered viva voce. In particular, this principle that I have just mentioned should prevail, but reference to prior, out-of-court statements of the witness may be allowed, as previously indicated by this Tribunal. Please do expect that in such cases this Trial Chamber will insist that such statements be read to the witness prior to him or her being questioned upon. And it brings me to the last point that I wanted to make. I have had the pleasure of working with you already for something like four, nine, plus three -- 12 hours, during sessions of the Pre-Trial Conference, and I have great expectations from you, but I also know that trials will always be trials, that there will be incidents, that not everything will be easy from beginning to end. Therefore, please allow me to draw your attention to certain rules of conduct that will be expected from you, and also please allow me to remind you of certain duties that are imposed on you both by Statute, by the Rules, as well as by the Code of Ethics that has been prepared. I will not be obviously exhaustive or deal with this at length, but I think also it is in the interests of your clients to hear what I have to say in open court. First of all, hopefully we will - and I do not anticipate that we will have to come to this - but please be reminded that in certain extreme cases, you may be subject to - I'm referring to counsel here, both sides - you may be subject to disciplinary proceedings under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, also as amended. And it is therefore necessary that you are aware of these -- of your rights and obligations as well as obligations towards this Tribunal. You also have a duty to keep your clients informed about the status of a matter before the Tribunal in which the client is an interested party and must also -- in other words, you also have a duty to promptly comply with all reasonable requests for information from your clients. It's important for me to remind you also that you must at all times comply with the Rules and any rules as to conduct and procedure as may be applied by the Trial Chamber in the course of the trial. You are expected also to have due regard to the fair conduct of proceedings. Something which is important and which I have no reason to doubt but which I am reminding you of just the same, you may not, unless permitted by the Rules or your Code of Ethics or by any of us three or the Chamber hearing this trial or any matter related thereto, make contact with any one of us three without first or concurrently informing counsel acting for the other party to the proceedings. You also may not submit exhibits, notes, or documents to us without communicating them first or concurrently to counsel acting for the other party. We will be on the watch-out for something which is fundamental -- fundamentally important for the proper conduct of proceedings, namely, that you are never expected to make an incorrect statement of material fact -- of a material fact to this Tribunal or offer evidence which you know to be incorrect. You also have a duty, and you are being reminded of this duty, to maintain the integrity of evidence, whether it is in written, oral, or any other form, evidence which is or may be submitted to this Tribunal. An appeal that we are making to you and which was also incorporated -- based on what is incorporated in the Code of Ethics is that you are expected to recognise all other counsel appearing or acting in relation to proceedings before this Trial Chamber as professional colleagues and you are duty-bound and therefore expected to act fairly, honestly, and courteously towards them and their clients. And this, of course, applies equally to the Prosecution as well as to the Defence. One very important rule of ethics which I emphasise is that you may not communicate with the client of another counsel except through or with the permission of that client's counsel. Finally, something which in trials of this nature is perhaps more important than in normal trials that we have in our home jurisdictions: I expect you, both the Prosecution and the Defence, again, to show the utmost courtesy towards witnesses, both in examination-in-chief as well as -- and as well as in cross-examination. You are, of course, free to examine and cross-examine witnesses to the best of your ability and in the way you deem fit and proper and also considering the attitude that each witness takes in any particular moment. But dealing adequately with a witness is one thing; failing to show courtesy or resorting to practices which will not be acceptable to this Tribunal, such as undue aggressiveness towards the witness, will not be allowed. Also, you will not subject witnesses to any unnecessary and unwarranted harassment. I'm sorry to have taken all this time in going through all this, but I think it gives me the opportunity and my colleagues the opportunity to more or less direct you from the very outset as to what to expect in certain circumstances when it comes to any of the aspects that I have touched upon. I think at this point in time I will look more to my left and call upon you, Ms. Korner, to make your opening statement. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I raise a matter before we begin that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I arrived this morning, I found in my locker this stack of additional disclosure from the Prosecutor. I told you last week in one of our Status Conferences that this trial was not ready to start, and one of the reasons it was not ready to start was that there are thousands of pages of material yet to be disclosed to the Defence. Now, I understand that we are starting and that that is not about to change, but I do have a humble request. It will take about two days for me to catalogue this material, get it properly filed so that I can find it again, and then read it in a way that I can understand it. So what I would request is that any time a series of documents of this magnitude -- there's a lot of documents here. There may be - I haven't counted the pages - seven or eight hundred pages, I don't know. Any time a pile of documents of this magnitude is served upon us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I may have the wrong glasses -- I may be wearing the wrong glasses, but I don't think there are 700 pages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it may be. It may be double-sided, I haven't looked. But in any event, however many pages there is, I think I may take a significant amount of time just to get through and to understand it, and to read it, and to get it properly filed. And so I would suggest that any time we receive a large number of documents like this, we have to stop whatever we're doing in terms of preparing for cross-examination of witnesses, we have to stop all the preparation we are doing for coming in here for trial, and get these catalogued and understood as to what effect they might have on the next cross-examination that we're going to be doing. In addition, there are new materials here for the first witness, Donia, who we just got this morning. Now, so what I would suggest is that any time we get materials like this, which should have probably been given to us months ago -- we're constantly getting materials that it's obvious from looking at them have been in the Prosecution's possession for months. So that any time we get this, I would request that the Chamber give us a two-day recess of the trial so that we can prepare for the next witness or whatever and have time to process these documents and become familiar with them, because it's of no value --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you the specifics of those documents? What documents are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't looked at them, so I don't know. They're disclosure documents that were given to the Prosecutor. And apparently they believe it's important and should be disclosed to us. Whether they're Rule 68 material -- some of them have to do with -- I know some of them have to do with Witness Donia, who is the next witness coming up. And if they're not important, then we shouldn't be given them. We have to treat them as if they are important. We have to treat them seriously. We have to read them carefully. We have to compare them with other similar documents on similar issues in the case. And at the same time, the Chamber expects us to be prepared to cross-examine the next witness, and I don't know how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are -- may remind you or draw your attention that you are falling into a contradiction here. Not last Monday but the sitting before - that's Friday's - when we were discussing the 800-odd pages of transcripts of the evidence that Mr. Donia had given in other trials and a question arose as to how important they were or whether it was wise to keep them or whether to withdraw those documents, Mr. de Roux was very open about this and said it's the case that the Prosecution withdraws these documents. They're not important. We don't want them. The Prosecutor was prepared to withdraw those documents and you weren't. And now you're saying if these documents that we have today are not important, why do we have them, why should they be in the records of the case, why should they occupy our time? I mean, decide, please. I mean, but however, irrespective of this -- because obviously you're making a complaint which may have -- may carry a lot of weight, I would like to know from the Prosecutor what documents Mr. Ackerman is in receipt today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assist on that. One of the problems, as Your Honour will recall, that we've discussed over the last few hearings is translations. One of the major problems is a diary that was received by the Prosecution some months ago. And Your Honour will recall I explained that the Translation Unit had offered or said they could translate some 300 pages. The bulk of the material that Mr. Ackerman and Mr. de Roux have received this morning are further translated pages of the Banja Luka diary. There are three translations of documents that will be referred to by Dr. Donia, and those are the only documents that refer to him. It is a problem that will arise throughout this trial because of the backlog of translations. If the situation is that Mr. Ackerman doesn't want to receive the translations as they come in, then of course we won't provide them. But if he does - and I anticipate that of course he does - then they will be coming in either in dribs and drabs or sometimes in bulk. We try to ensure the documents that will be referred to by witnesses have been disclosed or translated in advance, but it's not always possible and mistakes may arise. That is the situation in respect of the documents to which Mr. Ackerman refers today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the three documents that Mr. Donia will be asked to refer to or make reference to in the course of his testimony, what documents are they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't give -- I can't describe to you exactly what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How voluminous are they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think quite -- yes, Mr. Cayley has been dealing with this matter. Perhaps he can answer the question, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. They are very brief documents in respect of Dr. Donia. The reality in his report is that there are, I think, some 237 footnotes. All of those footnotes in the report make reference to books, publications, and documents, and some newspapers. The only documents that we intend to offer in evidence are what I would strictly call documents, rather than newspapers or books or other publications, and we have disclosed all of those up to yesterday, apart from three, which, for pure human failure, which is my fault, were missed going through the footnotes. The documents -- I think the longest document is two pages long, that was disclosed yesterday. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not a technical problem. It is not only a translation problem in this particular case. The Prosecution is tendering a private diary kept by a certain person. We have read it, and we have said that a private diary consists of daily impressions, and the Defence would like to see the totality of this document, because it is quite obvious that such and such a daily reaction is important and can be interpreted in different ways. That is why this is a problem of substance. But we have never had access to this document in its totality, though we have been asking for it for months, and we are now being given a part, a selected part, selected by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Prosecution, and we are told that this selected part, though we don't know the part that has not been selected, is going to be used for asking questions to the first witness. I think that if we begin this trial in this way, we are making a bad start. utterances.text: Your Honour, before I commence my opening statement to Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I commence my opening statement, may I just return for a moment to Your Honour's helpful remarks as to how the trial will be conducted? And may I ask, at the end of today, that I can raise one matter because it may affect tomorrow's witness? But Your Honours, with that in mind, may I now start what I have to say to Your Honours about this case? Your Honours, in 1992, the region which was known as the Autonomous Region of Krajina - in shorthand nearly always referred to as the ARK - was the scene of one of the most concerted, violent and ultimately successful campaigns of what is euphemistically described as "ethnic cleansing." It goes without saying that there is no such thing in law as "ethnic cleansing." Conduct which that term describes encompasses the range of offences which are set out in this indictment. At its lowest, it is the denial of fundamental human rights, rights of employment, of freedom of movement, the right to proper judicial process, moving through deportation, destruction of towns, of villages, of religious and cultural edifices and homes; going further, the detention of persons in camps in which beatings, torture, rape, sexual assault of women in general, and incidents of murder are a daily occurrence; and finally, killings, not only of single individuals, but of groups, some of them in the hundreds. All of those crimes which I have enumerated, the evidence will show, were committed in this case by Bosnian Serbs, of which the two accused form a part, and also by Serbs from Serbia and Montenegro. These crimes were committed by them upon the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations who, for generations, had been their neighbours. The greater part of the evidence that Your Honours will hear deals with the crimes committed against the Muslim population. That is simply because, in the areas which will be covered in this case, they formed the greater part of the non-Serb population, a greater part than the Croats. That is not to say that the Croats received better treatment, simply that there were less of them. What was the reason for these crimes? The Prosecution say that on the evidence of what was said and what was done by the accused and others, that the motive - and I emphasise that - the motive for these crimes was to create a Serbian state within Bosnia and Herzegovina, or at least to make it part of a wider Serbian state. And in order to establish that state, the intention - and I emphasise that - was to permanently remove the non-Serb population from the areas which had been designated to be part of that state and to effect the permanent removal by the commission of the crimes which are set out in this indictment. We submit that the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats were the object of these crimes for no other reason than that they were Muslim or Croat. The Prosecution suggests that once the evidence has been heard in this case, the Court will be satisfied that the crime of persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, as well as the other crimes which are enumerated in Article 5 of the Statute, were committed. However, we go further. We suggest that the evidence shows that in some municipalities, the ferocity of the methods used to remove the non-Serb population, the scale of the killings, or the targeting of the leadership in those municipalities, the beatings, the incarceration in detention camps, the deportations, the attacks upon and destruction of homes and villages, demonstrate an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations in part by destroying sections of the non-Serbs in the ARK area. In simplified terms, the Prosecution submits that the accused are therefore criminally liable for this genocide, for that is what the Prosecution say that it is, for four reasons: First, they intended the destruction of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in part in order to fulfil the aims of the objectives of the criminal enterprise where persecutions alone would be insufficient to achieve the desired result; or alternatively, the natural and foreseeable consequence of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly and permanently remove non-Serbs was that genocidal conduct with the requisite intent would be committed; or further, alternatively, the accused as superiors within the meaning of Article 7(3) knew or had reason to know that genocidal conduct was about to be committed with genocidal intent and did not prevent or punish the perpetrators thereof; or finally, as accomplices, they knew that principals were committing genocidal conduct with genocidal intent. Thus we say, we submit to Your Honours, that as against certain sections of the non-Serb population in the ARK, the aim of the campaign of persecution - in other words, to rid the area of non-Serbs - was realised through genocide. The accused, the Prosecution submit, bear criminal responsibility for this genocide because (a), they intended it; (b), it was a natural and foreseeable consequence of the criminal plan; (c), they knew or had reason to know and did nothing to prevent it happening; or they aided the principals in the commission of this crime. The evidence will show that both accused were not only close to the highest level of leadership within their respective spheres -- in other words, Radoslav Brdjanin in the political sphere; General Momir Talic in the military -- but also both exercised influence and authority within the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The political and military wings of the Bosnian Serbs were inextricably linked. The political arms provided the goals. The military played its part in the achievement of those goals. But they could not have done so without the logistical support of the political arm. Moreover, we submit that on the evidence that Your Honours will hear, it is clear that the military leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, of whom General Talic was one, shared the ideologies of their political counterparts. The role of the police in this enterprise in the events that took place in the Bosnian Krajina was no less important. In effect, they straddle the divide between the political and the military wings. They played their part in their civilian role by carrying out orders to disarm the non-Serb population, by carrying out arrests of what were considered to be undesirable persons, leaders of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations. They staffed the camps. They provided personnel to conduct interrogations. And Your Honours will hear the type of interrogations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that were involved. In respect of the military, they provided support by raising battalions of fighting men, sometimes known as "special forces," who acted under the command of the military. The concentration on the police may not be as great in this case as it might otherwise have been for one simple reason: Also charged in relation to these events in the Autonomous Region of Krajina is a man called Stojan Zupljanin, about whom Your Honours will hear quite a lot in this case. He was head of the State Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, known as the CSB. He is not on trial before Your Honours because, as of today, he has neither been arrested nor has surrendered. But as I say, his name will figure fairly large in this case. Your Honour, with those introductory remarks, before I move to some detail, perhaps I can explain briefly the purpose of this opening statement and start with the negative, as it were. This is not intended to be a complete rehearsal of all the evidence which Your Honours are going to hear in this case. I see Your Honour smile. It would take days and days and, in our submission, wouldn't be particularly helpful. Our case has, in any event, been very fully set out in writing in the Pre-Trial Brief. It goes without saying that Your Honours will be arriving at your decisions at the end of this case on the evidence that you hear and not what the Prosecution says to you about it. What we are going to do is merely anticipate what we think the evidence will be. We do not intend at this stage, other than the submissions that I have addressed briefly because it was important that Your Honours and the accused understand how we put the case of genocide, because it is the most important charge and the first time that it has been applied in this Court to such a wide-ranging set of events. Your Honour, therefore, we will not be addressing you any further on the elements of law. We won't even be mentioning the vex topic of international armed conflict. Your Honour, the purpose is really this: to prevent -- I'm sorry, to present to Your Honours an overview of the evidence which we anticipate will be given, to look at some of the context in which it arises, and some of the themes which arise from that evidence. Ultimately, in making this opening statement, we've had to make a selection. But we would say, and stress before Your Honours, that simply because a particular aspect of the evidence or a particular theme is omitted in this opening, it does not mean that we do not consider it to be an important part of the evidence. This opening is intended as a guide to the evidence which will come from witness testimony and from documents. Your Honour, may I very briefly outline the, as it were, biography of each accused in turn. Radoslav Brdjanin was born on the 9th of February, 1948, so he's now aged 53, very nearly 54. He was born in the municipality of Celinac, which is outside Banja Luka, and about which Your Honours will be hearing evidence. He was by profession a civil engineer who worked in the construction industry. In November 1990, in the first multiparty elections in Bosnia, he stood as the SDS candidate for Celinac, and he was elected to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In April 1991, an association called the Association of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities, known in its acronym form for -- in the Serb language as ZOBK, and I won't attempt to pronounce the actual words in the Serb language. But this association was set up. The President was a man named Vojo Kupresanin, again a man about whom Your Honours will be hearing in this case, and the Vice-President was Radoslav Brdjanin. In September 1991, that association became transformed into the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but the positions of President and Vice-President remained as before. On the 5th of May, 1992, there was on official announcement of the formation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Regional Crisis Staff. Radoslav Brdjanin became the President. Kupresanin was simply a member of the body. In due course, Your Honours, we'll have a look at the actual document. On the 15th of September, 1992, Brdjanin was appointed a Minister for Construction, Traffic, and Utilities, and became a Vice-President of the Republika Srpska, as by then the Serbian state within Bosnia had become known. And just to complete matters, he was arrested in Banja Luka on the 6th of July of 1999. Your Honour, Momir Talic, he was born on the 15th of July, 1942, so he's now aged 59. And he was born in Piskavica in the Banja Luka municipality. In 1961, he joined, as it then was, the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, as a professional military officer. By July of 1991, he had attained the rank of Colonel and he became the Chief of Staff or deputy -- and Deputy Commander of what was then known as the JNA 5th Corps, which was stationed in Banja Luka. And later, he was promoted to the rank of what we would call Major-General, but I think in the Serb language is General Major. On the 19th of March, 1992, he was appointed the commander of the 5th Corps. When on the 19th of May, 1992, the Bosnian Serb army was established, known as the VRS, the 5th Corps of the JNA became the 1st Krajina Corps, often shortened to 1st KK. On the 31st of December, 1991, he was promoted to General Lieutenant and he remained as commander of the 1st Krajina Corps throughout the conflict in Bosnia, until Dayton. In February of 1998, he was appointed Chief of Staff of the VRS by Biljana Plavsic, who was then the minister in charge of the army. And he still occupied that position, that is Chief of Staff, when he was arrested in Vienna on the 25th of August, 1999. Your Honours, may I now turn to the background to these events? We suggest it is impossible to understand these events, about which evidence will be led in this case, and more importantly, the role of the accused in these events, without some explanation of the background so that those events and those roles can be looked at in context. Although any starting point to a certain extent must be an arbitrary one, to most of the witnesses in this case, it is the elections which were held in November, 1990, which first brought clearly into focus the developing nationalistic trends. The majority, if not all, witnesses will say that before, and for a period after the elections, the three major ethnic groups in Bosnia - that is to say the Serbs, the Muslims who later became known as Bosniaks, and the Croats - had lived together in harmony. Many worked together and, particularly in urban areas, there was a great deal of intermarriage. In those elections, three main parties emerged. The Serb party was the SDS; the Bosnian Muslim party, the SDA; and the Bosnian Croat party, the HDZ. It was the SDA who won the most seats in the Republic Assembly, followed by the SDS and then, last, the HDZ. Again, it may be a reflection of the fact that the Croat populations in Bosnia and Herzegovina were in fact smaller than the Muslim. The remaining seats were split between other parties, which included the former Communist party. When looking at the events of this case, it is also worth keeping in mind that many of the trappings of the communist system remained very much in place. All those who gained or took authority in the early 1990s, and most of the persons who were subjected to that authority, were products of that system. Control of the media was made simpler because traditionally those in charge of radio and television stations were political appointees. The directors of commercial enterprises were still largely political appointees. Most such enterprises in the early 1990s still remained politically controlled. Privatisation, as you will hear from witnesses, was very much in its infancy. Accordingly, for example, an order which was issued that management posts in the Krajina enterprises must be filled by persons who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was an order issued on the 11th of May by the ARK Regional Crisis Staff, was a relatively simple order to put into operation. 1991 saw the break-up, or the beginnings of the break-up, of Yugoslavia. I know that Your Honours are probably very familiar and so I propose to deal with that -- these events very briefly. On the 25th of June, 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence, following referenda which had been held in their respective republics. The JNA left Slovenia after a mere ten-day war. In Croatia, the conflict between the JNA, assisted by irregular paramilitary forces, began in June of 1991 and lasted until January of 1992, when, as a result of international pressure, the JNA largely withdrew into Bosnia. The conflict in Croatia had a significant impact in Bosnia as a whole. A mobilisation call had been issued. The Bosnian Serbs responded but, on the whole, the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims did not, and that caused a great deal of ill-feeling. More particularly, in the municipalities with which this case is concerned, those which were situated on or near the border with Croatia, in those municipalities, the buildup to the takeover of control by the SDS began at an earlier stage. It became clear that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be following Slovenia and Croatia on the path to independence. The SDS did not wish to take this path. On the 24th of October, 1991, they formed their own assembly. It was a meeting attended by, for example, Krajisnik, Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic and Radoslav Brdjanin, and indeed the first speech after the introductions had been made was, in fact, one made by Radoslav Brdjanin. Your Honours, throughout the SDS assemblies which were held between that date in October and in particular the 12th of May, 1992, although obviously they continued thereafter, none of the leaders who spoke made any secret of their intentions, which can really be summed up in the document that was issued after the 12th of May assembly. It is one of the tragedies, the Prosecution suggest, that people did not listen closely enough to what was being said. Your Honours, it may be appropriate at this stage to take the break because what we propose to do now is to show you a short video clip of that assembly on the -- of the 12th of May.

utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Could I ask that the first page be put up so Your Honours can see how it's headed? Your Honour, this, of course, is a translation. There are a number of copies of this document. This is copy number 96, headed "Instructions for the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances." Your Honours, if we could put the next marked page on? Your Honour will see the reason for these instructions in due course. I have no doubt, in the light of what Mr. Ackerman says, that Your Honours will be having a fairly close look at this document, but if we go to the bottom, paragraph number 4: "In order to ensure uniform and prompt implementation, the establishment of the tasks, measures and other activities are to be established in accordance with Variants A and B, and in two stages." I think if we go to the next marked page, Your Honour will see - and I'm not going to go through that too much - but Variant A. Variant A was to apply to municipalities where the Serbs were in a majority, Variant B to municipalities where they were not. And for these purposes, item 3 is the most important. "The SDS municipal board will immediately form a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people in the municipality comprised of the following," and you will see the various descriptions of the persons who were supposed to be on the Crisis Staff. I will return to the question of Crisis Staffs later. Finally, can I ask for one more page to be put up? There were variations, and -- yes, I don't think that's, unfortunately, the -- although it's worth looking at item 8 on this. "Intensify information and propaganda activities in order to inform the Serbian people, in a timely and complete manner, about the political and security situation in the municipality and beyond." Your Honour, the question of propaganda is something that I will be dealing with as a separate topic. I think it's just the last -- the last page. Is that the last page? All right. I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's the difficulties of doing -- could I just have a look at the document for a moment? Your Honours, I would draw Your Honours' attention to item paragraph 7: "The Crisis Staff is responsible for special forms of defence organisation on the territory of the municipalities where Serbs are not the majority population, and the Crisis Staff is obliged to continually monitor the situation within the municipality as well as the broader political, military and security developments. It also has a duty to promptly initiate and take actions which are appropriate to any given situation and its possible developments." Your Honour, that paragraph was specific to the Variant B phase. It is couched in anodyne language, as so many of these documents that Your Honours will look at were, but the Prosecution suggest that it was effectively giving these so-called Crisis Staffs carte blanche to deal with the situation in the way in which, as we shall see, they did. Yes, thank you very much. Your Honour, having heard Mr. Ackerman's objection to the authenticity of this document, Your Honours may find it somewhat surprising - it's happened before, and I believe it's happening in another case at this present time in this Tribunal - because those instructions were published in full in March of 1992 in a newspaper called Slobodna Bosna. In addition to that, in 1995, Karadzic made a speech in which he referred to these instructions. It was a speech to the 50th assembly of the, as it then -- by then was, Republika Srpska, and he said this: "You will remember the A and B Variants. In the B Variant, where we were in a minority," and he said 20 per cent or 15 per cent, "we had set up a government and a brigade." And the rest of the speech doesn't matter, but we suggest clearly he cannot have been referring to anything other than those instructions. And we say those instructions were a basic blueprint for what was to follow and what was done. On the 29th of February and the 1st of March of 1992, the Bosnia-Herzegovina government held its own proper, if that's the right word, referendum in respect of whether or not they were to declare their independence. The SDS urged the Serb population to boycott the referendum, and for the most part, they did. Muslim and Croat voters in Bosnia participated and the result was a vote in favour of declaring independence. The European Community had recognised the independence of Slovenia and Croatia on the 15th of January of 1992, and in the light of the referendum in Bosnia, they stated - that is to say, the European Community stated - that it would recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state effective from the 6th of April, 1992. And it is that date that it could be said marked the real beginnings of the conflict. Your Honour, can I turn now to a little bit -- before I move to the question of what was the Autonomous Region of Krajina, to deal with a little bit about the background in relation to the military side as it affects General Talic? I've already told Your Honours that in 1991, he was the deputy commander of the JNA 5th Corps and took command around the 19th of March of 1992. Now, the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was later renamed the VRS, was officially created on the 12th of May of 1992, that is as part of the assembly meeting, and General Ratko Mladic was placed at the head of the army. As I've already also said, Talic remained as the corps commander throughout the war in Bosnia. Looking at the background of the transformation of the JNA into that part that became the Bosnian Serb army, it would appear that the aims of the JNA in the early part of 1992 were to maintain Bosnia as part of a federal Yugoslavia. Equally, they made it plain that they wished to protect the Serb areas of Croatia and to prevent ethnic conflict within Bosnia so that it did remain within the Yugoslav state. Now, the announcement of Bosnian independence, the international recognition thereof, and the growing independence of the legitimate Bosnian government, made the aim of keeping Bosnia within Yugoslavia apparently an unattainable one. And once Bosnia had been recognised as an independent state, this effectively transformed the JNA into an army of occupation - it was the Yugoslav National Army - and in particular, an army of occupation to those who opposed it. However, to the Bosnian Serbs, it appeared as a protector. And Your Honours will see in the documents many references to the JNA being told that they needed to remain to protect the Serbs. And during this very tense period, assisted really by nationalist propaganda and partly by self-interest, it would seem, there was a clear convergence of interest which developed between the Serb party, the SDS, and the JNA in Bosnia, in particular in the early months of 1992. And in order to overcome the issue of the JNA being seen as an army of occupation, key decisions were taken to transform the JNA in Bosnia into a predominantly Serb army so as -- so that the interests of the Bosnian Serbs could be protected. And incidentally, of course, the aims of the SDS would be furthered if they had an army in their support. As far as the 5th Corps was concerned, in the spring of 1992 -- between January and the spring, in the early part, it was initially operating in fighting in Western Slavonia - that's in Croatia - where it had been deployed in late 1991. And the justification for the operations there were later characterised as that of protecting the Serbs in that part of Croatia from genocide. As Your Honours will hear, "genocide" was a word that was bandied about with a great deal of freedom by all parties in this period. As the United Nations cease-fire was implemented in Western Slavonia and concurrently the situation in Bosnia deteriorated, the 5th Corps began to redeploy forces into what were anticipated to be crisis areas and municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina area. This included the moving of units and artillery into what were perceived to be potential flash-points. In a similar manner to the JNA as a whole, the 5th Corps initially viewed the deployment in Bosnia as one to reduce ethnic tensions within the area. But as this became increasingly unlikely, the position of the 5th Corps began, as we say, to converge with the position adopted by the SDS, and increasingly it became a corps that backed the SDS political line in the Krajina area. We have looked very briefly at the video of -- that was -- or part of the video of the proceedings on the 12th of May. It is clear that the military were present and in the forefront of the ranks of people who attended. There were two key areas of discussions and announcement: First, a declaration of the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs; and secondly, the establishment of the Army of the Serbian Republic, the VRS. Those strategic goals which were announced in that meeting laid out the blueprint, effectively, of the establishment of that Serbian state which, for convenience sake, I will call Republika Srpska although that was not the original way it was described. They defined the borders of that state and the territory that they claimed - the Bosnian Serbs claimed - was theirs and, most importantly, laid out the type of state it would be; in other words, a predominantly Serb state. And in essence, the so-called ethnic cleansing campaign can be in part tied to this meeting and the goals which were announced at that meeting. Your Honour, I believe we've got -- we may not have -- a copy -- no, we haven't. Your Honours, perhaps we will in due course be looking at that document. The strategic goals were as follows: separation from the other two national communities; the establishment of a corridor between the Bosnian Krajina and Serbia -- again, Your Honours will hear a lot of references to "the corridor" in this case. That was the area which lay between Krajina and that of Serbia itself -- the establishment of a corridor in the Drina Valley; and the establishment of a border on the Una and Neretva Rivers - I still have a lot of difficulty with the names - division of Sarajevo; and finally, access to the sea. The establishment of a Serb army included an official establishment, the renaming and integrating of Territorial Defence units - TO as they were known - into the VRS; the establishment of units and commands; and the appointment of Mladic as the chief of staff. And it brought together, that meeting, the military and the political bodies, together in a set of shared common goals. And those goals, as we say, produced, as a natural consequence, really, the, as I say, so-called ethnic cleansing. Can I deal very briefly at this stage also with the formation of the 1st Krajina Corps. There was a large-scale mobilisation and expansion of the corps throughout 1992. Integrated into it were the Serbian municipality Territorial Defence units, which became Light Infantry Brigades. Talic in fact maintained the same corps headquarters and staff bodies that had existed when it was the 5th Corps, and he maintained many of the JNA units that had existed as part of the 5th Corps. They had gained combat experience in Western Slavonia and had also acquired much of the military hardware. The corps really was one of the strongest and best equipped of the whole of the VRS. It became, by the end of 1992, one of the larger if not the largest corps of the VRS. And what was stressed was the cooperation with civilian bodies at both municipal and regional level, cooperation with police at the same levels, and the removal of Muslims and Croats from positions of authority in the military at the same time as they were being removed from businesses and political office. In brief, the 1st Krajina Corps, under the command of General Talic, conducted a series of operations during the summer and autumn of 1992. Those operations were designed to seize control of territory which had been designated as Serb, whether or not in actual fact at that stage it was occupied largely by Serbs. The operations were carried out to assist in the separation of the ethnic communities, operations to secure the borders and boundaries of the state, and to defend that territory once it had been seized. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Those military operations were publicly said to be justified to protect the Serbs from genocide. In fact, there were a number of municipal-level combat operations to take control of the territory within the municipality and to crush any non-Serb resistance. There were also larger scale military operations designed to secure key terrain or objectives. One example was called "Operation Corridor" which successfully did in fact restore the link between the Krajina and Serbia. In respect of the municipality attacks, they really followed a pattern, and I shall come back to the question of pattern a little later. The pattern was as follows: There was a moving in of forces prior to the attacks, including artillery and armour. Deadlines were issued. There were then swift and overwhelming response to flash-point incidents. There was shelling, attacks, killings and retaliatory incidents. The population was rounded up. They were removed to detention camps, and the consequences thereafter were deportation or killing or whatever, or beatings; all the matters that are referred to in the indictment. There was commendation of these units after the actions. Your Honours, I will deal a little later with the question of resistance, but I want to make it clear straightaway at this stage, the Prosecution does not suggest that there was no resistance to what was happening. There was. And it may not be surprising in the circumstances. Your Honour, as far as looting is concerned, there was large-scale looting which was reported in military documents. It often took place after attacks, and it involved military personnel. Regulations were passed by the military to forbid individual looting, but effectively, when one looks at the regulations, it appears this was only because this type of looting stopped the Serbian authorities' appropriating property for the state coffers. And the issue of propaganda, which I will return to again, that was just as common within the military as in the political sphere, and the themes were very, very similar. The themes were that there was a threat of genocide against the Serbs, that the army was the protection of the Serbs against genocide or an international Muslim-Croat conspiracy. Your Honours, as far as command and control is concerned, which is obviously an important issue as far as General Talic is concerned, he had a functioning corps headquarters with all the staff branches that would be recognised in any military command; that is to say, operations, intelligence, security, morale, logistics. And many of the staff officers who had been in the 5th Corps went straight into the 1st Krajina Corps. In order to ensure a functioning corps headquarters and to ensure that the passage of information was facilitated, Talic used the following methods: There were weekly and ad hoc briefings with his corps star officers; there were briefings of lower level commanders; there were daily combat reports, written orders and instructions, requests for information, visits to units and formation of the corps, and verbal as well as written instructions. And General Talic, as is probably the same in any army all over the world, passed and received information from his superior command, which was the main staff of the VRS, in a similar manner. The JNA regulations were effectively adopted in the VRS. They set out the role and duties of a corps commander. It is the single, most important position within the hierarchy of a corps, for the purposes of absolute responsibility, authority and accountability. That was the corps commander. The foremost duty of the corps commander was to actively command the forces under his control, and according to the regulations - and this is a brief summary - the right to command units and institutions is under the exclusive responsibility of the commander. He bears the responsibility for the accomplishment of a mission. He takes decisions, gives assignments to his subordinates, organises coordination and cooperation, and controls the implementation of decisions. He is responsible for harmonising the activities of his command, subordinated commands, and headquarters. And, in particular, where there are combat actions, he is responsible for integrating the organisations in the assigned zones. He was legally and individually required, and I quote, "to control the work of the corps" -- I'm sorry, "control the work of the corps command, assign tasks to his subordinates, make sure that they were carried out, and bear full responsibility for their completion." He could authorise officers from the command to command units or to take decisions or to sign reports, but he still bore the full responsibility for the work of those units or officers. He was required, in his reporting instructions, to monitor constantly the situation in the zone of combat and support -- I'm sorry, and report to his superior commander. And so, as can be seen from the documents which were kept by his own corps, he required subordinates to keep him informed, via frequent and regular reports, of all activity and developments relevant to the corps. And he himself filed reports with his superior command. As far as discipline is concerned, the corps commanders were provided with a wide range of legal and disciplinary powers to maintain and ensure - and this is a phrase we've all heard before - proper military discipline and the conduct of subordinates. And military discipline and order were recognised by the JNA as basic requirements for the achievement of military objectives. The corps commander was individually vested with the legal and administrative tools necessary to maintain order and punish violation of military regulations, orders and laws. And those regulations provided that the corps commander could employ proceedings ranging from disciplinary action to court-martial to the actual initiation of criminal proceedings. And a military prosecutor's office and a military court were established by the VRS and were functioning by the autumn of 1992. And finally, the laws of war. The corps commander was specifically made individually responsible to ensure the compliance of his units with the international laws of war. He was obliged to institute criminal proceedings for violations of international and domestic laws, and was expressly tasked with ensuring that his - that is, Talic's - corps command organs and subordinates' commands, units and institutions are working within the law. We say that these and other applicable sections of the regulations are unambiguous. They leave no room for a corps commander to doubt his personal responsibility and liability for violation of the laws of war committed by himself or units under his control. And Your Honours, we say that, in this case, the evidence will show gross and flagrant violation of those laws. Your Honours, can I turn now to the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Throughout the period that this case is concerned with, it underwent various changes of name, some official, some not. The body was referred to as a Crisis Staff, sometimes as a Crisis Committee, sometimes as a War Staff, sometimes as a War Presidency. The instructions to change the name sometimes came from the leadership. But whatever name it went under, it was the same body. The nature of it remained the same. Your Honours, we hope, will hear from people more expert in the constitution and the laws of Yugoslavia than certainly I am, but the Crisis Staff body appears to have been derived from the laws of national defence which had been enacted by the former Yugoslavia and within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. That allowed this body to perform all the functions of the assembly during a state of war or in the event of immediate danger of war. The functions of the assembly would, in fact, be assumed by the presidency, so that the presidency could make the laws that normally the assembly would make. Once the state of emergency was over, any such decrees or laws would be -- would have to be submitted to the assembly for ratification.
