utterances.text: This is the version that went into the Official Gazette, which I believe came out late or later. There is, as I say, another version, but I'm not going to trouble to show it to Your Honour at the moment because, although there are some changes from the official publication, it only arises in relation to some people at the end. Your Honour, if we can go through the list, then, Radoslav Brdjanin was President of the ARK Crisis Staff. Vice-President, Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic, the gentleman I pointed out in the video of the 12th of May, who was sitting, as one looked at it, to the right of Talic. The third name, Vojo Kupresanin, member; and as I said to Your Honour, in every other case, I think, in the municipalities, it was always the president of the assembly that became president of the Crisis Staff. Here, for whatever reason, Vojo Kupresanin merely was a member. The next man, Nikola Herceg, who actually signed this, he was the minister of the executive council - I'll get the right term in a moment - but in any event, a leading light in the politics. Predrag Radic was the president of the municipal assembly, sometimes described as the mayor of Banja Luka. People who met him, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particularly from the international community, when talking about the mayor, would mean him. Dr. Radoslav Vukic was a doctor. He was also the president of the regional SDS board. And I think -- I mean, I wouldn't like to swear to that -- but he was the gentleman in the video with the beard. Dr. Milovan Milanovic [phoen] was, I believe, just a doctor. Eight, General Momir Talic. Nine, Major Zoran Jokic. He was the air force. Ten, Stojan Zupljanin was the head of the CSB, the state security station in Banja Luka. Dr. Rajko Kuzmanovic, was director of Banja Luka University. Milan Puvacic [phoen], I'm afraid to say I can't remember what his function was. Jovo Rasic [phoen] was the president of the court in Banja Luka. Nenad Stevandic [phoen] was, if I can call it, the youth wing of the SDS. I cannot also remember who Mr. Bulic was. But Nadzelko Kezic [phoen] the head of the DSB, which was, I suppose, was the equivalent of the Secret Service intelligence network. So as Your Honours can see, using Variant A and B, people were on this Crisis Staff from all walks of life, as it were, all walks of the leadership within the Krajina. Yes, thank you very much indeed. How did the Crisis Staff operate, or Staffs? There seems to be little doubt that meetings, particularly in the early stages, were held virtually every day. For some of the municipalities, the Office of the Prosecutor is in possession of the minutes which were kept of those meetings. That is not the case in respect of the Regional Crisis Staff meetings, but we do have copies of the decisions, some, as it were, in their original form with stamps and signatures and some which appear through the gazette. And it's certainly clear from those that the meetings were extremely regular ones. The Crisis Staffs dealt with every aspect of life in the municipalities, from the most mundane to the most serious. And the meetings of the municipal staffs show regular contact with and meetings with local leaders -- I'm sorry, local military leaders. Now, the role of the ARK Crisis Staff, the regional one, was defined by itself in a series of decisions which it issued in May of 1992. On the 9th of May, it said this: "Decisions adopted by the war staff of the Autonomous Region are to be strictly respected in all public and economic organisations." On the 18th of May, 1992, it dealt with the role of the Crisis Staffs in the municipalities, stating: "The Crisis Staffs are now the highest organs of authority in the municipalities." And the 26th of May, 1992, it said this: "The work of the Crisis Staff of the ARK has absolute support, since it is now the highest organ of authority in the ARK. Decisions of the Crisis Staff are binding for all Crisis Staffs in the municipalities." Now, the point has been made effectively on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin that any body - and I mean by "any body," any public body - can declare itself the highest authority. But if no one takes any notice of what it says, then it can declare itself whatever it likes; it's a joke. Leaving aside the fact that so many of the witnesses who will testify will give evidence to the effect that, as far as they were concerned, the Regional Crisis Staff was the voice of authority, the Prosecution say that the evidence will show that it did have authority, that it was not a joke. Stojan Zupljanin, on the 6th of May, the day this decision was announced, called a meeting of the chiefs of the municipality public security stations, short form SJBs. In that meeting, which was documented, he told them this: "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the ARK Crisis Staff." In the municipalities themselves where we have copies of the minutes and decisions, one can see the decisions made by the Regional Crisis Staff having an effect. For example, in Sanski Most, on the 7th of May, 1992, the local Crisis Staff there implemented three decisions which had been made by the Regional Crisis Staff the previous day. As far as Kljuc was concerned, they prepared a report in July of 1992 dealing with their activities over the period until then. And in that report, they said: "The conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff were binding as regards all issues connected with life and work in that municipality." In Kotor Varos, in July -- events in Kotor Varos started a great deal later than in the other municipalities and continued a great deal later. There is evidence in a document that the ARK Crisis Staff appointed a coordinator to be in charge of dealings with the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff. The documents show that members of the ARK Crisis Staff attended meetings at the municipality level and vice versa. These decisions and conclusions make it absolutely clear, it should be said, that the relationship between the ARK Crisis Staff and the municipality Crisis Staffs was not a straightforward hierarchical one. It wasn't an operational structure like the police or the military. It appears to have been a relatively new, untried, and untested system, and there seem to have been elements of improvisation. It does seem that the municipal Crisis Staffs were given a certain amount of autonomy. There weren't apparently strict reporting structures, as existed in the military, as I earlier outlined to you, nor a clearly delineated chain of command. The relationship between the municipality Crisis Staff, the police, the military authorities, the ARK regional Crisis Staff, and indeed at republic level, political and military and police, it was a symbiotic one, and certainly there seemed to have been instructions which may have bypassed what one might have thought was the ordinary chain of command. But even if the actual reporting chain was not a straightforward one, even if, in practice, the ARK Crisis Staff was not able to exert the total formalistic control and authority that it wished, the evidence will show that it had great influence on the course of events which took place in the area of the ARK through the decisions that it issued, and its role, if nothing else - and the Prosecution say it was more than that - as a coordinator and intermediary between the levels of the municipality and that of the republic government. Radoslav Brdjanin was the president of this body. The decisions -- the decisions which were issued by the Crisis Staff bore his name. Your Honour is aware already that there is some issue as to whether where his signature appears it actually is his signature. The Prosecution say that it is inconceivable that if one looks at the evidence of his relationship with the events which led to the establishment of this body, the public statements he made, his activities during the period of the indictment, and the position that he obtained after the abolition of the Crisis Staff, that he was no more than a figurehead. He was, we say, a politician committed to the goal of creating the Serbian state within Bosnia and Herzegovina -- in fact, so committed as to often be described as an extremist, and we say that, in the position which he occupied, he was able to advance that goal. In order for the Crisis Staff to have legitimacy and authority, it had to have, in its membership, the leaders of the institutions which had control or influence over events. Therefore, the police and military were vital components of that authority. Your Honour, I have already reminded or informed you of what Zupljanin said when calling a meeting of the chiefs of the local police stations. But can I turn to the question of General Talic's participation? His connection and role, or his connection with and role in, the ARK Crisis Staff has been the subject of a great deal of debate and legal motions in the pre-trial process. We say that his part in the joint criminal enterprise was carried out largely through his position as Commander of the 1st Krajina Corps. But in order for the ARK Crisis Staff to have proper legitimacy and carry weight, it had to have, as part of its membership, the leader of the military. He may not have attended many of the meetings. There is certainly a reference in one of the documents to General Talic being requested to attend meetings or to send a member of his staff. There is no evidence - and I make it absolutely clear - that he participated in the discussions which led to the taking of decisions. There are no minutes. The municipal minutes do show that the military at that level attended meetings and participated in the discussions. But, as I say, we have no evidence in respect of General Talic doing the same. There is, however, some evidence that his assistant -- sorry, his Assistant Commander for civilian affairs, a man named Colonel Vojnovic, did attend at least one meeting, on the 12th of June, when the position of the Muslim and Croatian officers who remained in the corps was discussed. And moreover, at no stage did General Talic ever disassociate himself from that publicly-announced position as being a member of the ARK Crisis Staff. He could have done so, had he wished. The rector of Banja Luka University, Mr. Kuzmanovic, whose name Your Honours saw, did in fact resign and was replaced by another member of that university. No doubt, had General Talic resigned, as he realised, he might well have dealt a body blow to the united front that the Bosnian Serbs were seeking to present to the international community, that this was a combined political-military action, that they were acting as one. The ARK Crisis Staff was not a stand-alone institution. It was but one of the power structures that were put in place, we suggest, to achieve the goal of that Serbian state. It did, in fact, have a relatively short official shelf life, if that's the right term, because it was formally declared to be in existence in May of 1992 and, theoretically at least, was wound up in July, the 17th of July, when the ARK assembly met to ratify its decisions, the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff. In September of 1992, the Republika Srpska constitution - and I use the Republika Srpska simply as the name that eventually was adopted - was amended and the Serb Autonomous Regions, the SAOs, were abolished so that government became centralised. There wasn't this layer, then, of regional activity between the municipalities and the republic level. And thereafter, Radoslav Brdjanin played his part in the pursuit of that goal as a minister and Vice-President of the government. General Talic continued as the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps and continued to act in that capacity. Your Honour, can I turn now to the development of the events themselves and the pattern? Your Honour, I said earlier that if the world had listened to what was being said in the assemblies and meetings, it would have been quite clear what was intended by the Bosnian Serbs. There was one particular speech made by Radovan Karadzic on the 15th of October which really couldn't have made it clearer. And I'm going to ask that that be shown to Your Honours now. It's a short excerpt. Your Honour, it comes from The Death of Yugoslavia programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I -- thank you. Your Honours, as I say, it couldn't have been clearer what was intended. Although there are variations in the themes and in the dates, effectively the pattern of events in the establishment of SDS control in the municipalities was broadly similar. The amount of force that was used depended very much on whether the municipality in question had an overall Serb majority. In an extremely simplified version, Your Honour, because of course, there are gradations and grey areas and sophisticated areas -- sophisticated differences, but the progress of events roughly followed this course: There was proclaimed in the municipality an Assembly of the Serbian People. Although the process began as early as 1991 in many places, the weapons which were held by the territorial units in their various depots, and indeed in factories and the like, were taken over by the JNA, and these weapons were then distributed to Serbs, ordinary Serbs. Next, a demand was made by the authorities that all non-Serbs should sign an oath of loyalty to the Serbian state which had been proclaimed. And they're supplied first and foremost to the members of the police. Those who did not comply, immediately lost their jobs. The next step was that the Serbian Assembly transmogrified itself into a Crisis Staff. On the 1st of May, a call for mobilisation was issued within the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina by Lieutenant Colonel Sajic, the gentleman we saw. And I've now got his correct title; he was secretary of the Council for National Defence within the autonomous region. At the same time, an order was issued -- this is within the same order -- that all paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally possess weapons and ammunition are to immediately and by 1500 hours on the 11th of May, 1992 at the latest, surrender them to the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence or to the nearest public security station. This order to surrender weapons was perhaps one of the most significant of all the issue orders given. It acted, we suggest, as a catalyst for the outbreak of violence. It was coached, it may seem, in rather neutral terms, that people in possession of illegal weapons should hand them over, as should paramilitary formations. As I said earlier, many of these decisions did appear to be in neutral terms. In fact, in its execution and in its intention, we say, it was directed solely at the non-Serb population. That deadline of the 11th of May was extended later to the 14th of May and, in some municipalities, to a later date, but all in May. After the expiry of that deadline, the Serb forces moved into the non-Serb areas. Can I give two examples of how this worked from municipalities both of which came within Talic's area of responsibility. In Prijedor, from the 23rd of May onwards, military attacks were carried out by the combined forces of the 1st Krajina Corps, army reservists from Prijedor, reserve police officers from Prijedor, together with paramilitary units. The major attacks which took place were on the Muslim villages of Hambarine, Kozarac, and Kamicani. In Sanski Most, on the 27th of May, 1992, the predominantly Muslim village of Hrustovo was shelled. It was shelled by units of the Serb army which, as I say, came under the control of General Talic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. On the 29th of May, the predominantly Muslim village of Vrhpolje was attacked. In Kljuc, the municipal Crisis Staff issued a final ultimatum for the surrender of weapons to the police by the 28th of May. The shelling of Muslim villages began that very afternoon. The mention of Kljuc brings me back to the question of resistance, which I touched upon when dealing with Talic's responsibilities. As I say, it is no part of the Prosecution case to suggest there was no resistance to what was happening. In Kljuc, in the village of Krasulje, there was a clash between Muslim villagers and a Bosnian Serb police patrol. In that clash, the Serb police commander was killed. It appeared to act as a kind of signal for the attacks to begin. In Kotor Varos, to take another example, the village of Vecici mounted an armed resistance to the Serbs for a number of months, and there were, throughout the municipalities, individual acts of resistance. However, the Prosecution suggests that the resistance that there was in response to a threatened and later actual widespread attack upon the Muslim and Croat civilian population. It is true that some non-Serbs obtained military weapons. Sometimes, in fact, as you will hear, they were sold to them by Serbs who had acquired them when they were being distributed and who were later able to provide the information to the police as to who of the non-Serb population was in fact in possession of a weapon. Many of the Muslims and Croats had authorised personal weapons, hunting rifles and pistols and shotguns and the like. The order that was issued to disarm talked about illegally-held weapons. People actually held these weapons legally with permits. Hunting was apparently a way of life, particularly in rural areas of Bosnia. In many cases, the non-Serbs themselves set up village patrols and set up checkpoints around their neighbourhoods. But, we submit, all of this was done in response to these threatened attacks. In most, if not all cases, the resistance offered to the Serbs was insignificant and hopeless, particularly when confronted with the reality of the superiority of weaponry and trained manpower which was available to the Bosnian Serbs through the support given to its corps by large numbers of the JNA, now transformed into the Bosnian Serb Army. The Bosnian Serb leaders from the very top of the republic level to the municipality level at the lower had made their intentions clear. They threatened non-Serbs with violence; not only with violence, but with, we suggest, expulsion and possible extinction. And so those who were threatened responded to the best of their limited ability. These acts of resistance were exaggerated by the Serb media and used as a justification by the Bosnian Serbs for them to say they were acting in self-defence and for them to mount a widespread and systematic political, military and police campaign against the non-Serbs. I've described the attacks which took place in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. In places where these kinds of attacks were unnecessary, in the sense that the Bosnian Serbs formed an unassailable majority or they were able to terrify the population into leaving - as happened certainly in the time of Donji Vakuf - the pattern followed the course of really denial, to begin with, of rights, dismissals of non-Serbs from their employment. In many cases, that meant a loss of the houses because the houses were tied together with the employment. Barricades and checkpoints were set up, preventing any freedom of movement by non-Serbs. The police and/or armed Serbs, sometimes members of regular military forces, sometimes paramilitary formations, and sometimes simply local Serbs, neighbours of the people who were threatened, who put on a uniform and carried weapons, moved into the Muslim and Croat villages. In some cases, individual arrests were made. There was, it appeared to be, a clear targeting of men who were leaders of the community. In other cases, there was a whole-scale rounding up of the inhabitants of a particular village. People were forced to leave their homes, which were subsequently looted and then damaged or destroyed by explosion and/or burning. Populations were separated into men other than the elderly, those over the age of 60 or 65, and women and children. The men, some of them were taken first to the police station, where they were interrogated. And before, during, or after - and sometimes all three - such interrogation, they were beaten. From the police stations, they were taken to camps. Others were taken directly to camps, some of which were temporary accommodation, others of which were more permanent. And in due course, I want to have a look at camps in a little more detail as a particular topic. Women and children were also taken to camps, and the conditions were almost without exception substandard. And indeed the word "terrible" is not one that is an exaggeration. Removal of the non-Serb population was the aim of this campaign of terror. By and large, the methods were remarkably successful. Many fled before or after the attacks. As I've said now, I think twice, in May of 1992, most of the Muslim population left the town of Donji Vakuf. In other municipalities, convoys were organised. In Bosanski Novi, for example, in July of 1992, the officials from UN organisations who were present across the border in Croatia were virtually blackmailed into agreeing to assist with the transportation of hundreds, if not thousands, of Muslims from the area. Many of the people who had been detained in the villages and towns, if they were not placed into camps, were forcibly marched to places such as Travnik, and from there, they were taken into Croatia. And those who were detained in camps, once released, were also forced to leave the territory. To add insult to injury, before leaving, non-Serbs were forced to sign over their property and they were equally strictly limited on the amount of valuables they could take with them. In June of 1992, the ARK Crisis Staff issued a decision that anyone who tried to leave with more than 300 deutschmarks would have the surplus confiscated, in inverted commas. In essence, they were giving a licence to steal. People who tried to leave would be searched and all their valuables would be taken from them. On the 19th of June, the Crisis Staff stated that all, in inverted commas, abandoned property, was to be proclaimed property of the State. As I said earlier, one of the reasons for attempting to stop the military looting was the fact that the State wasn't gaining the benefit of that property. And in essence, the Prosecution says that the evidence shows a pattern of acts occurring across the municipalities which are the subject of this case. It is submitted that the similarity of the events shows that they did not come about through happenstance but were designed as part of a coordinated campaign, the objective of which was to remove the non-Serbs from the areas which the Serbs considered to be Serb territory, and more than that, to make sure that those who were not killed or locked up somewhere, never came back to those areas. Your Honours, the next theme I want to touch upon is the question of propaganda, which I raised earlier on. Propaganda is defined by the Oxford English Dictionary - and I hope that people will forgive me for using a dictionary native to my country - as an organised programme of publicity, selected information, et cetera, used to propagate a doctrine or practice. And it couldn't be a better description of what happened here. Of course, the use of propaganda in itself is not a crime, but it was an integral part of the buildup to the events in this indictment, and in its most extreme forms, at the very least, creates a climate whereby people are prepared to tolerate the commission of crimes, and at its worst, propaganda can act as an incitement to commit crimes. The Serb leadership was fully alive to the importance of control of the media. Decisions were taken at both the republic and regional assemblies to establish Serbian radio and television stations. One of the earliest events in the ARK which was noteworthy, which occurred before the period of this indictment, was the seizure of the transmitter on Mount Kozara, which took place in August of 1991. After that seizure, the communities which were served by the transmitter could only receive television broadcasts from Belgrade, Banja Luka, Novi Sad and Pale, all of which were strongly Serb. The seizure was, in fact, carried out by a Serb paramilitary group from Prnjavor, about whom Your Honours will hear something. It was known as the Wolves of Vucak, but it was assisted by the chairman of the executive committee of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, a man named Anjelko Grahovac. In one of the first decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff on the 6th of May, the media was ordered to "furnish maximum information on the developments in the Serbian Republic." Radio stations, such as those as Banja Luka Radio and Prijedor Radio, had their non-Serb employees replaced by Serbs who effectively would follow the party - in other words, the SDS - line. At its most basic level, the propaganda took the form of always describing the Muslim population as extremists or Green Berets or Turks, and more vulgarly, balijas. Croats were always the Ustasha, referring back to the Second World War. In its most extreme form, it reached the very height of vileness, and if we could just show Your Honours one page from a document which was issued. If that could be put on the ELMO? Your Honour -- if we could can see the top of the page? Thank you. This was a publication entitled, "The Informater" and was issued by the SDS party in Sanski Most in July of 1992. And it begins: "Dear brother Serbs, do you know what our bloodthirsty enemies have been scheming for us? What they had in mind was to gouge out our eyes and carve us up, hack our bodies to pieces, rape women and girls in front of their dearest, to circumcise, to destroy our religion, to crush us, just because we happen to be Serbs. Don't ever think that anybody's family would have been spared. They had monsters ready and committed to raping Serbian women and they had developed a system of killing each and every Serb. Soon we will show everyone their horrible weapons, the swords from the Middle Ages, sledgehammers, special knives, instruments to gouge out eyes with and instruments to carve us up. A decent man shudders with horror. In Vrpolje, a Ustasha killed his own two young children, then turned around to shoot at the army. When one of our soldiers fell into their hands, he was butchered in the most beastly manner. They had been preparing for genocide against the Serbs but did not get away with it because we saw what was coming. We warned and prepared our people in time. The leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party are resolute in their undertaking to accomplish all the Serbian people has entrusted them with. Dear brothers, the war is not over yet." It is almost inconceivable, standing here in this courtroom, to believe that something like this could be issued and let alone that anything like this could be accepted. However, in the climate of the times, it was something that people did believe, apparently, and that type of propaganda was there for one reason, and for one reason alone; to encourage the ordinary Serbs to believe that they were under serious threat from these vile enemies and to take the appropriate action. According to witnesses, Radoslav Brdjanin, together with Dr. Vukic, made some of the more inflammatory speeches on radio and television. Brdjanin's most oft-quoted statement was to the effect that only a small percentage, the figures vary between 2 and 5 per cent, of Muslims should be allowed to remain in Banja Luka. And it became clear to the people who heard his statements that the reason for him doing so was to terrorise the non-Serbs into leaving. Nor, it has to be said, was Momir Talic above using that type, although not as extreme, of inflammatory or derogatory language. He gave a TV interview in 1995. He gave a number of interviews, but in this particular one, he was asked whether the fact that there had been no genocide in his area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, was due to a genetic memory or the readiness of the corps? And he said this - and of course accepting this is a translation into English: "Well, I think you mostly answered the question," this to the interviewer. "This generation was taught not only by history but by its parents and grandparents, what the Ustasha knife means, what the knife of the Turk convert means." Your Honours, as we said earlier, it wasn't just that the military was doing what it was told by its political masters. It actually shared the views and ideology of other Serbs. Can I turn now to the topic of the camps? The Serbs had to find places to put the non-Serbs who were being driven from their homes and/or being detained. So in each municipality, they set up places of detention, sometimes euphemistically described as reception centres, and if we could just put up on the screen a map which gives an overview of the number of these camps? Is it on Your Honour's screen? It's not on mine. Technological wizardry sometimes doesn't work. Do Your Honours have it? Do Your Honours have the map? No, they don't.

utterances.text: Yes, it is. Is it possible to fix it? Yes, I'm afraid that isn't very helpful. Your Honour, the place with the -- perhaps one can see it. You will see there's one municipality which has the largest number of camps, roughly above the centre of the picture. That's Prijedor. But I don't think, unfortunately, it's come out terribly well. And I shall promptly blame my technological expert who did this. Well, I'm sorry about that, but perhaps that -- it gives a general picture of the camps. And Your Honour, may I say that that is just the major camps, not what I described as the temporary makeshift ones. Your Honour, the treatment which was meted out to the detainees is set out very clearly in the indictment in paragraph 42, and I'm not going to rehash it. At its very lowest, it could only be regarded as inhuman. Overcrowding, lack of sanitation, insufficient food, limited if any medical treatment. The male detainees were regularly submitted to -- or subjected, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rather, to humiliating rituals. That was the lowest. They were beaten, sometimes so severely as to lead to death. And torture was not uncommon. Camps were established in factories, schools, football stadiums. Some were the temporary transit type; others more permanent. The guards on the whole were police or military or a mixture of both. Can I deal in a little detail with just two of the camps? Prijedor contained some of the worst examples in Keraterm and Omarska, both of which have been the subject of recent trials in this institution. Keraterm was established on the 23rd of May in a disused factory in the town of Prijedor itself. It was disbanded on the 21st of August. It was the site of one of the more notorious killings in this area because on the 24th -- around the 20th of July, some 150 to 200 civilians were brought to Keraterm. They were detained in room 3. Some four days later, they were fired upon and killed by Serbs who were using machine-guns. It was acknowledged by the camp commander, Sikirica, when he tendered his plea of guilty to the offences, that apart from that killing, other individuals had also been killed in the camp. And detainees in that camp were tortured and brutally beaten. Omarska was operational from the 27th of May of 1992 until the 21st of August, 1992, when it was finally disbanded, although the majority of its inmates were moved out in early August. According to the records kept between the 27th of May and the 16th of August, a total of 3.334 persons were brought to, as it was described, the Omarska Investigation Centre. Of those 3.000-odd, some 37 of them were women. For the first days of its operation, the camp housed many of the local Muslim and Croat elite: the political, the administrative, the religious, the business leaders. Many of these people were beaten on arrival. On a daily basis, virtually serious assaults and killings took place. Detainees were made to beat each other, and many of the assaults took place in front of other persons detained. Women were raped or otherwise sexually assaulted. Analysis of Serb documentary evidence shows that a large number of those 3.300-odd people are still unaccounted for. Many were taken from the room in which they were being held and never seen again. Bodies were seen in areas of the camp before being loaded onto trucks and removed. And that camp was visited by members of the ARK Crisis Staff, who included Radoslav Brdjanin. Now, it was the visit of the ITN news crew on the 4th of August, 1992, to this camp and to another camp called Trnopolje which first drew the attention of the world to what was actually happening in Bosnia. And Your Honour, I think it's worth reminding ourselves very shortly just of some of the footage that was shown on television. May I say that we have in one part edited out the sound where there was allegations being made by people who were behind the wire. We've only dealt with the parts where we don't think there's going to be a dispute. So I wonder if I could -- we could just have a quick look at that.

utterances.text: "Most have been here for two months. They say they don't know why, that they were rounded up from their homes. They were too frightened to talk about the way they have been treated and the conditions in which they have been kept, conditions which have been hidden from the world, as the Serbs have denied access here to the United Nations and to the International Red Cross. Their prison is an old mining complex outside Banja Luka in Northern Bosnia. In an office above the canteen, the camp commandant and the spokeswoman for the local Serbian authorities said they have two and a half thousand of what they called internees who were being interrogated as possible Muslim fighters." "No, this is not a camp. This is a centre, Omarska and Trnopolje. Both centres, not camps." "The prisoners were being brought to the canteen from a large industrial building in the centre of the mining complex. It, too, was under heavy guard. And we asked to be allowed to look inside. But in spite of promises of openness from the Serb Bosnia leader, Dr. Karadzic, we were told we could see no more." "Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us?" "He promised us something else and said, 'You can do this and this, and that, and not that.'" "Our armed escort made it clear. Our visit was over. We are now being asked to leave this camp, having seen nothing more than the canteen. We have been told that Dr. Karadzic's promise, while good to us, does not carry any weight here. "As we were moved on, soldiers told us the army did not control the camp, which they said was run by the local authorities and militia. We had asked to be taken to a second camp, at Trnopolje in the same area, to which several hundred prisoners from Omarska had last day been transferred and which had also been at the centre of allegations of atrocities. Conditions at this camp were appalling. In 100 degree heat, hundreds of men were forced to eat and sleep outside in a field, behind barbed wire. Their meagre rations consist of a small hunk of bread and a bowl of soup every day. Here, too, they said they had been rounded up, whole villages emptied of their men, and they were afraid. "In the makeshift medical centre, there were cases of scabies, malnutrition, and diarrhoea. Local doctors said they were chronically short of medicine and drugs. Among them was a Muslim doctor. We asked him whether there had been any cases of beatings." "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, interestingly enough, the day before that visit, on the 3rd of August, General Talic sent an order to Manjaca camp command to the Prijedor - which I will come back to in a moment - to the Prijedor 43rd Brigade and the Prijedor police, ordering them to make conditions satisfactory in Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm because of a forthcoming visit to the International Community and media. Your Honour, the Prosecution say that he and Brdjanin were well aware of the conditions of these camps. After the visit of the television crew, most of the detainees were transferred either to Trnopolje or to Manjaca. Manjaca was a 1st Krajina Corps detention facility. It was on a JNA or VRS training ground which was south of Banja Luka. From June until December of 1992, thousands of civilians were detained in animal stables. Part of the ground was a farm. Juveniles and sick prisoners were detained with men who were aged between 18 and 60. Conditions in the camp were inadequate. Prisoners were frequently and systematically beaten, beatings which caused severe injuries and sometimes death. Again, Muslim intellectuals and leaders appeared to be targeted. In June of 1992, a group of prisoners was brought from Sanski Most. Six of them were killed directly outside the camp. In August, another group was transferred from Omarska. They were beaten on their arrival at the camp by their police escort, and many of them died. The camp was visited at the end of August 1992 by an international delegation led by Sir John Thompson. The mission was accompanied by members of the European Community Monitoring Mission, as it was then known, ECMM. And Your Honours will hear from two of these monitors their impressions of the camp. They were, to say the least, appalled. Although interestingly enough - and it is a sad reflection on what happened - to many of the people in Manjaca who had come from other camps, particularly that of Omarska, the conditions were themselves almost bearable. Manjaca was controlled and staffed by the 1st Krajina Corps. The camp commander reported directly to General Talic and many documents demonstrate that Talic was aware of the details of the facility and was personally involved in its operation. General Talic did allow visits by a Muslim humanitarian organisation called Merhamet, but it is not clear what happened to the food and clothing which was delivered. The International Committee of the Red Cross made an inspection in July of 1992. One of General Talic's officers, Lieutenant Colonel Vukelic made a report on that visit to the general. He said that the Red Cross had been critical of the conditions and had demanded the release of some of the prisoners who were clearly ill. Colonel Vukelic's recommendation was that, in future, they should ask for two to three days' notice before the Red Cross carried out any such inspection. Manjaca was certainly visited by Kupresanin, and there is some evidence to suggest that it was visited by Radoslav Brdjanin. Brdjanin's view on the camps was apparently expressed in a TV programme at the end of August, when he appeared and stated, "If Hitler, Stalin and Churchill could have working camps, so can we. We are at war." Your Honour, perhaps before we can break, I can -- if Your Honour would care, agree to break, I can deal with one more topic and then I can complete what I have to say tomorrow. I don't think it will take me more than an hour or so. Your Honour, can I turn to the topic of destruction, in particular religious and cultural destruction? And there should be another map which may or may not appear on Your Honours' screens and may or may not be visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are waiting on the map, can I just advise the Chamber that I have a short oral motion that I would like to make for your consideration before we leave today? And I think it's important timing-wise that I make it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could close now? I could [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you stop now for the moment and resume tomorrow, and we could deal with the point that you wish to raise and also the oral motion that Mr. Ackerman would like to raise as well. Shall I start -- shall we start with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was simply this. It's a very simple point. Your Honour, describing the situations in which leading questions might be asked, and obviously dealing with the obvious that if it's done by agreement or so on, Your Honour, in respect of experts, where an expert has prepared a report in which he gives his opinion which is an analysis of documents and the like, Your Honour, we would submit the normal practice is that -- simply to get through quicker, is that he may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what I failed to state or add this morning was that there will be moments when I myself will realise or come to the conclusion that I would direct you or it could be Mr. Ackerman or it could be Mr. de Roux to forget about non-leading questions and put a direct question. There are instances where that becomes convenient. It doesn't wreak any havoc or cause any prejudice to anyone. So rest assured, we will use our good judgement. This is not an area which is new to any one of us. I understand what you say. I mean there will be moments, however, where on the basis of what I have read from General Talic's note in response to your request for admission of adjudicated facts, where more or less I am in a position to tell you go ahead, you can put a direct question here, or more or less, no, let the witness say what he has to say and please don't put any suggestions to him. I mean, we will direct it as -- I know -- I can imagine what the problem is. It will arise not only with expert witnesses, it will arise with other witnesses as well. One uses the experience that we all have in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was hoping, as I think I raised with Your Honour at the last Pre-Trial Conference, was that the Defence counsel will agree to meet with me before a particular witness is called or to indicate in open court which areas will not be in dispute and therefore which evidence may be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, that is an exercise that this Chamber will also be doing on its own, in preparation of the interim Status Conferences that I suggested, recommended yesterday -- the day before yesterday, sorry. It -- I'm studying it at the moment, and I don't think it should be a very controversial or a very difficult exercise. However, I must point out to you that you're not to expect that on what you think or thought or indicated could be easily admitted as adjudicated facts, there is going to be either the consensus on the part of the Defence. Much of that material is controversial, inherently controversial, and you're never going to get the consensus of the Defence. There will be other adjudicated facts that the Chamber itself will intervene upon and admit them, probably ex officio or motu proprio. We will deal with that as we go along. And I'm also sure, going through the response of General Talic in this regard, that there are also other points, material facts, that they are not contesting, which -- there are not many and -- but they are still material facts, and provided we are all aware of them, it could -- they could be helpful in reducing the time required by several witnesses in giving evidence. But anyway, I think we need to cooperate, you and the Defence bench, in any case, but also together with the Tribunal, I'll try to help you in that direction, and I don't think the exercise should be that difficult. But don't expect, I repeat, that all that you thought initially could be admitted as adjudicated facts could easily be admitted as adjudicated facts. I mean the Tribunal, the Chamber itself, does not agree with you in many, many respects.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, we are lost, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we will face that as we go along. I mean, because it's no use taking a document which is that thick and telling you -- I mean, waste more time than gain any mileage out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I then - very quickly because I know -- so I don't eat into Mr. Ackerman's time - I do want to mention something about the question of hostile witnesses, but it's nothing urgent, but in relation to the Rule 92 witnesses, counsel for Talic put in a motion after we'd replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Having declined to give reasons in court. In respect, I don't think we need to deal so much with the matters in the earlier witnesses, but the dead witness, Your Honour, we would wish to -- well, we would seek to persuade Your Honours that he can be read, but I would prefer to do that, I think, as an oral argument. We don't require a prior ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that we do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I rise with some trepidation, Your Honours, because it seems that I'm always making some kind of points about the excessive work and how little time and things of that nature, but this one, I think, is really quite important and I'm actually trying to seek some guidance from the Chamber. In consideration of the time of Dr. Donia, what I would like to do, unless the Chamber has already decided otherwise, is to work extremely hard from now until Monday morning in the hope that I can be prepared by that time to conduct the cross-examination. I think if I work very hard at it between now and then, I can. That would mean, however, that another task that has been ordered that I perform by this Chamber, I wouldn't be able to do, and so I think it really has to be the Chamber's decision what priority I should place on these two matters. The first is preparing for the cross-examination. The second is a -- my -- the requirement that I supplement my Pre-Trial Brief with a response to the Prosecution's section on the law. I don't have time to do both of those things. I can do one or the other. My suggestion - and I think probably what makes the most sense in terms of time and everything else - is that I be given an additional couple of weeks to do the supplement to the Pre-Trial Brief because I think that is probably lower priority than trying to finish with Dr. Donia, rather than have him have to come back at a later date. But I'm asking for guidance. I'll do what the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, would an extension of the time limit already granted to Mr. Ackerman with regard to his deficiency in the Pre-Trial Brief disrupt your programme or cause you any undue prejudice?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so at all, Your Honour. I wanted Your Honour to order that he give us more detail of his Defence. I'm less interested in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this; I realise what Mr. Ackerman is mentioning now is indeed a real problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Ackerman, how much time do you require by way of an extension?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think probably an additional two weeks, Your Honour. I think we could probably have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber is giving you three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll probably use every bit of it, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I hope you also use the short break in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do nothing but work on this case, Your Honour. I promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure. So that brings our work for the day to an end. I am to understand that tomorrow you will conclude, Ms. Korner, your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will proceed with Mr. Donia. How long do you expect Mr. Donia to be on the witness box -- witness stand?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In chief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't assist because Mr. Cayley, as you know, is dealing with him, but I can make inquiries. My guess would have been certainly the whole of tomorrow's session, if I take, say, another hour tomorrow, the remainder, and possibly going into Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Chamber is still in possession of the disclosure materials that were given to me this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact, I'm going to return them now to you. I will not give you two days because I almost went through the whole of them in about 20 minutes the first time and about 20 minutes the second time. Most of them are photographs. Some of them you need to read because they are statements by, I suppose, witnesses that will be produced, but the rest is the diary that was mentioned earlier. Most of it is in the B/C/S language, which you don't understand in any case, and which your clients will have ample time to go through. Maybe there will be instances when new documents will be thrown on your lap later on which will require not just two days, even more, but certainly not this batch that you gave me this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, life will improve after Saturday because I will have a new case manager kind of person who can do a lot of this for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose what we did today should guide us for the future. When you have such a problem, please don't hesitate to raise it because it may be a very valid one. It could be very flimsy, like it happens to be today, but certainly it's not your fault because I concede that you had not read them before. Please, could you hand these back to Mr. Ackerman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll try to avoid raising flimsy things if I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not expect you to avoid raising such issues. You are duty-bound towards your client to raise such issues when they need to be but, you realise that had you waited until the break and did what I did, perhaps you could have kept silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, for much time now, I've been looking at this pile of documents that I haven't gotten to yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's frightening. And yesterday I saw a whole team of employees here coming into my Chamber with volumes and piles of paper, and I barely have space for myself in that room, let alone for all these documents that are flowing in. But anyway, that's not a problem. We will deal with it as we go along. Everyone has to organise oneself. And we will see. I thank you all for the cooperation that you have shown this morning. This is more or less what my idea of proper conduct of a sitting should be. There have been no interruptions. That's how it should be. And hopefully tomorrow, you will be able to conclude your opening statement within a short time so that we can commence with the evidence stage. I thank you and see you all tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 13.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of January, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
